parsed.study_design: Qualitative study using semi-structured interviews and thematic analysis
parsed.population_and_sample: Twelve local-government representatives from Tasmania's rural municipalities who had public-health responsibilities for managing drinking-water supplies
parsed.exposure: Local-government drinking-water governance and regulation under Tasmania's Public Health Act 1997, including regulatory obligations, financial and staffing constraints, infrastructure limitations, testing requirements, legal liability, and limited jurisdiction over catchment land uses
parsed.outcome: Provision and availability of safe drinking water, including untreated supplies, boil-water alerts, inability to meet regulatory standards, affordability constraints, and consideration of permanently discontinuing reticulated water service
parsed.rationale: The Methods section (p. 3) reports semi-structured interviews with 12 rural local-government representatives and thematic analysis, establishing an identifiable qualitative empirical design. The findings (pp. 3–6) link regulatory duties, liability, inadequate infrastructure, limited funding and staffing, and catchment-governance constraints to untreated water, boil alerts, affordability problems, and possible shutdown of community supplies. The Conclusion (pp. 7–8) explicitly identifies inequitable access to safe drinking water and institutional options for improving provision and regulation.
